prompt: What does oil palm processing involve?

options.text: Mechanical and chemical operations for extracting crude palm oil and palm kernel oil
Only mechanical operations, with no chemical step at any stage
Only the drying and storage of harvested bunches
The breeding of higher-yielding palm varieties

explanation: Mechanical and chemical together. Pressing is mechanical, chemical extraction of kernel oil is chemical, and sterilisation sits between the two.

why.a: Correct. Mechanical and chemical operations to extract CPO and PKO.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Palm kernel oil can be obtained by chemical extraction.
why.c: Wrong. Drying and storage are two steps in a much longer sequence.
why.d: Wrong. Breeding is part of propagation in the cultivation unit.

prompt: Crude palm oil is abbreviated {{1}}, and palm kernel oil is abbreviated PKO.
explanation: CPO. Module Three uses four abbreviations: CPO, PKO, PKC and POME, plus EFB and FFB.

prompt: Which set gives the five fresh fruit bunch processing stages in order?

options.text: Sterilisation, threshing, digesting, pressing, clarification
Threshing, sterilisation, pressing, digesting, clarification
Fibre separation, nut drying, cracking, extraction, storage
Propagation, nursery, field establishment, agronomy, harvesting

explanation: Sterilise, thresh, digest, press, clarify. The order is not arbitrary: sterilisation loosens the fruits so threshing can work, and threshing must precede digesting.

why.a: Correct. This is the order the text and the deck both give.
why.b: Wrong. Sterilisation comes first; threshing is of sterilised bunches.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the palm kernel processing stages.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the cultivation stages from Unit 1.

prompt: The last of the five fresh fruit bunch processing stages is {{1}}.
explanation: Clarification. Beware cracking and storage, which are stages in the kernel sequence rather than the fruit sequence.

prompt: How is sterilisation of palm fruits or bunches achieved?

options.text: By boiling, using steam under pressure
By chemical soaking in lime solution
By exposure to ultraviolet light
By freezing the bunches before milling

explanation: Boiling with steam under pressure, in pots, drums or sterilisation chambers as done in mills.

why.a: Correct. Sterilisation before milling is achieved by boiling, using steam under pressure.
why.b: Wrong. Lime is used in the fish farming unit to remove iron from water.
why.c: Wrong. No ultraviolet treatment appears in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Freezing is a fish value addition method, not a palm treatment.

prompt: What does sterilisation do to the fruit itself?

options.text: It disinfects the fruits by killing pathogens and inactivating the enzymes that could degrade the oil
It softens the shell so that the kernel can be cracked
It separates the oil from the water and sludge
It removes the fibre from the kernel

explanation: Kills pathogens, stops enzyme activity. Both matter for oil quality, because enzymes are what raise free fatty acids.

why.a: Correct. Disinfection and enzyme inactivation are the first stated purposes.
why.b: Wrong. Cracking follows nut drying in the kernel sequence.
why.c: Wrong. That is clarification.
why.d: Wrong. That is the fibre separator, in kernel processing.

prompt: Sterilisation inactivates the {{1}} that could degrade the oil.
explanation: Enzymes. Their action is what produces free fatty acids, which is the standard measure of poor palm oil quality.

prompt: Which two further purposes does sterilisation serve?

options.text: Loosening the fruits from the bunches, and reducing microbial contamination for better oil quality
Drying the nuts and improving cracking efficiency
Separating the mesocarp from the kernel
Skimming the sludge from the surface of the oil

explanation: Loosening and reducing microbes. Loosening is what makes the next stage, threshing, possible.

why.a: Correct. Both are named among the purposes of sterilisation.
why.b: Wrong. That is nut drying in the kernel sequence.
why.c: Wrong. That is digesting.
why.d: Wrong. That is clarification.

prompt: Sterilisation {{1}} the fruits from the bunches, making it easier to separate them.
explanation: Loosens. It is why sterilisation must come before threshing rather than after it.

prompt: At what temperature and for how long is sterilisation carried out?

options.text: Around 140 to 150 degrees Celsius for 60 to 90 minutes
Around 40 degrees Celsius for 70 to 80 days
Around 25 to 34 degrees Celsius for 12 to 15 months
Around 100 degrees Celsius for 10 to 15 minutes

explanation: 140 to 150 degrees Celsius for 60 to 90 minutes. Option B is the seed dormancy treatment, and it is the trap: 70 to 80 days against 60 to 90 minutes.

why.a: Correct. Steam under pressure at around 140 to 150 degrees Celsius for 60 to 90 minutes.
why.b: Wrong. That is how seed dormancy is broken before planting.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the growing temperature and the nursery period.
why.d: Wrong. Neither figure appears in the course.

prompt: Sterilisation uses steam under pressure at around 140 to {{1}} degrees Celsius.
explanation: 150. The pairing to hold is 140 to 150 degrees for 60 to 90 minutes.

prompt: How long does sterilisation take?

options.text: 60 to 90 minutes
70 to 80 days
6 to 9 hours
12 to 15 months

explanation: 60 to 90 minutes. Watch the units in every Module Three number question: minutes, days, months and years all appear, and the examiner mixes them.

why.a: Correct. Sterilisation runs 60 to 90 minutes.
why.b: Wrong. Days belong to the dormancy treatment at 40 degrees Celsius.
why.c: Wrong. No such figure appears.
why.d: Wrong. Months belong to the nursery period.

prompt: Where can sterilisation be carried out?

options.text: In pots, drums or sterilisation chambers as done in mills
In jute bags or oil tanks
In polythene bags in the nursery
In cold rooms with backup generators

explanation: Pots, drums, chambers. The range matters because it covers everything from a smallholder to an industrial mill.

why.a: Correct. These three are named.
why.b: Wrong. Jute bags store dried kernels and oil tanks store the oil.
why.c: Wrong. Polythene bags hold seedlings in the nursery.
why.d: Wrong. Cold rooms belong to the fish marketing unit.

prompt: Why is sterilisation described as crucial in controlling the oil's quality?

options.text: Because it minimises the formation of free fatty acids
Because it raises the oil's smoke point
Because it removes water from the crude oil
Because it darkens the colour of the oil

explanation: Minimising free fatty acids. High free fatty acid levels are the standard sign of degraded oil, and the enzymes that produce them are what sterilisation kills.

why.a: Correct. Sterilisation controls quality by minimising free fatty acid formation.
why.b: Wrong. The smoke point difference is between palm oil and palm kernel oil.
why.c: Wrong. Water is added during clarification, not removed by sterilisation.
why.d: Wrong. No colour change is claimed.

prompt: Sterilisation controls oil quality by minimising the formation of free {{1}} acids.
explanation: Free fatty acids, abbreviated FFA. The glossary defines them as substances that form when oil degrades, indicating poor quality if levels are high.

prompt: What is threshing in palm oil processing?

options.text: The removal of fruits from sterilised bunch stalks
The breaking of cell walls to separate mesocarp from kernel
The removal of fibre from the kernel
The heating of crude oil with water to remove sludge

explanation: Fruits off the stalks, after sterilisation. The deck adds that it improves digestion efficiency, because only fruit should reach the digester.

why.a: Correct. Threshing removes fruits from sterilised bunch stalks.
why.b: Wrong. That is digesting.
why.c: Wrong. That is the fibre separator in kernel processing.
why.d: Wrong. That is clarification.

prompt: Threshing removes fruits from the bunch {{1}}, and improves digestion efficiency.
explanation: Stalks. What is left after threshing is the empty fruit bunch, one of the three by-products.

prompt: Fruits digest easily when they are hot and well sterilised.
explanation: Stated directly in the threshing paragraph, and it explains why sterilisation and threshing run straight into digesting rather than being spread over days.

why.true: Correct. The text says fruits digest easily when hot and well sterilised.
why.false: Wrong. This contradicts the stated reason for keeping the sequence tight.

prompt: What does digesting do, and what is the process also called?

options.text: It breaks down cell walls to separate the mesocarp from the kernel, a process called de-pulping
It boils the bunches to kill pathogens, a process called sterilisation
It presses the pulp to release oil, a process called extraction
It dries the nuts before cracking, a process called curing

explanation: De-pulping: breaking cell walls in a digester so the oily flesh comes away from the kernel. The deck adds that it improves oil extraction efficiency.

why.a: Correct. Digesting breaks down cell walls to separate mesocarp from kernel, that is de-pulping.
why.b: Wrong. That is sterilisation, the first stage.
why.c: Wrong. That is pressing, the fourth stage.
why.d: Wrong. Nut drying belongs to kernel processing, and curing is not a term used here.

prompt: Digesting mills sterilised fruits in a {{1}} to break down the cell walls.
explanation: A digester. Each stage has its own machine: thresher, digester, press, clarifier, and for kernels the fibre separator and cracker.

prompt: How do you know digesting is complete?

options.text: When no streak of coloured outer skin remains distinguishable
When the oil begins to separate from the water
When the nuts reach a low enough moisture content
When the free fatty acid level falls below a set threshold

explanation: No streak of coloured outer skin left. It is a visual test, and a very quotable one.

why.a: Correct. This is the completion test the text gives for digesting.
why.b: Wrong. Oil and water separation is clarification.
why.c: Wrong. Moisture content governs nut drying.
why.d: Wrong. Free fatty acid level is a quality measure, not a completion test.

prompt: Digesting is complete when no {{1}} of coloured outer skin remains distinguishable.
explanation: Streak. It is the text's own word, which is what makes it examinable as wording rather than as understanding.

prompt: Which three presses does the text name for extracting crude palm oil?

options.text: Screw presses, hydraulic presses, and centrifugal presses
Roller mills, hammer mills, and ball mills
Sand filters, carbon filters, and iron-removal filters
Digesters, threshers, and clarifiers

explanation: Screw, hydraulic, centrifugal. They apply high pressure to the digested pulp to release crude palm oil.

why.a: Correct. These three presses are named in the text.
why.b: Wrong. Those are grinding mills, not palm presses.
why.c: Wrong. Those are water treatment filters from Module Two.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the machines of other processing stages.

prompt: The presses apply high pressure to release crude palm {{1}}.
explanation: Crude palm oil, CPO. What remains after pressing is palm pressed fibre and the nuts.

prompt: What happens during clarification?

options.text: The crude palm oil is mixed with water and heated to separate solids such as fibres and sludge, by boiling and skimming
The fruits are boiled to kill pathogens
The kernels are cracked and sorted
The oil is bleached and deodorised

explanation: Water plus heat, then boiling and skimming. The deck sums it up as separating fibre and sludge from the oil.

why.a: Correct. Water and heat, boiling and skimming, to separate solids from the oil.
why.b: Wrong. That is sterilisation.
why.c: Wrong. That is cracking, in the kernel sequence.
why.d: Wrong. Bleaching and deodorising are refinery steps not covered in this course.

prompt: Clarification separates solids from the oil by boiling and {{1}}.
explanation: Skimming. The glossary describes clarification as heating and skimming to separate oil from water, solids and impurities.

prompt: What happens to the clarified oil?

options.text: After cooling it is stored in containers for proper packaging and marketing
It is returned to the digester for a second pass
It is mixed with palm kernel oil before sale
It is discharged as effluent

explanation: Cool, store, package, market. Poor storage after this point causes oxidation and rancidity, which is the last of the four quality factors.

why.a: Correct. The clarified oil is cooled and stored for packaging and marketing.
why.b: Wrong. Digesting happens before pressing, not after clarification.
why.c: Wrong. The two oils are separate products with separate processing lines.
why.d: Wrong. POME is the effluent; the clarified oil is the product.

prompt: Which set gives the five palm kernel processing stages in order?

options.text: Fibre separation, nut drying, nut cracking, kernel oil extraction, storage
Sterilisation, threshing, digesting, pressing, clarification
Nut cracking, fibre separation, storage, drying, extraction
Propagation, nursery, establishment, agronomy, harvesting

explanation: Separate the fibre, dry the nuts, crack them, extract the oil, store it. Drying must precede cracking, which is the ordering point the examiner is most likely to test.

why.a: Correct. This is the kernel sequence in order.
why.b: Wrong. That is the fresh fruit bunch sequence.
why.c: Wrong. Cracking cannot come before fibre separation and drying.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the cultivation stages.

prompt: The palm kernel sequence begins with {{1}} separation.
explanation: Fibre separation. The fibre removed here is the palm pressed fibre, used for biomass energy and animal bedding.

prompt: What machine separates the fibre from the kernel, and is there an alternative?

options.text: A fibre separator, and the manual method can also be used at this stage
A digester, and there is no alternative
A hydraulic press, and the manual method is forbidden
A clarifier, and only mills can perform it

explanation: A fibre separator, with the manual method available. The glossary defines it simply as a machine that removes fibre residues from the palm.

why.a: Correct. A fibre separator, or the manual method.
why.b: Wrong. The digester breaks down the mesocarp before pressing.
why.c: Wrong. Presses extract oil; the manual method is explicitly allowed here.
why.d: Wrong. Clarification is a different stage entirely.

prompt: A machine called a fibre {{1}} is used to separate the fibre from the kernel.
explanation: Separator. The manual method can also be used at this stage, which the text says explicitly.

prompt: Which three drying methods does the deck give for palm nuts?

options.text: Machine drying, hot platform, and sun drying
Freeze drying, vacuum drying, and spray drying
Boiling, skimming, and pressing
Mulching, shading, and hardening off

explanation: Machine, hot platform, sun. The self-assessment answer shortens it to sun drying and mechanical drying, which are the two the examiner is most likely to want.

why.a: Correct. These three drying methods are named on the deck.
why.b: Wrong. None of these appears in the course.
why.c: Wrong. Those are steps in the fruit processing sequence.
why.d: Wrong. Those are nursery practices from Unit 1.

prompt: Nut drying reduces {{1}} content and improves cracking efficiency.
explanation: Moisture. The self-assessment answer adds a second benefit: it reduces kernel breakage during cracking.

prompt: Why is nut drying necessary before cracking?

options.text: It reduces moisture content, making cracking more efficient and reducing kernel breakage
It sterilises the nut against fungal attack
It raises the oil content of the kernel
It softens the shell so that no machine is needed

explanation: Lower moisture, better cracking, fewer broken kernels. Broken kernels are worth less, so the drying step pays for itself.

why.a: Correct. This is the in-text answer word for word.
why.b: Wrong. Sterilisation of the fruit happens much earlier.
why.c: Wrong. Drying removes water; it does not create oil.
why.d: Wrong. Cracking machines are still used; drying makes them work better.

prompt: Several types of machines and processes are used in the cracking and sorting of palm kernels, once they are dried to a lower moisture content.
explanation: Stated directly. Note the condition attached: once they are dried, which is why nut drying precedes cracking in the sequence.

why.true: Correct. The text describes several cracking and sorting machines used after drying.
why.false: Wrong. The text says several types are used, and ties them to dried nuts.

prompt: By what two methods is palm kernel oil obtained from the kernels?

options.text: Mechanical pressing and chemical extraction
Boiling and skimming
Threshing and digesting
Sun drying and hot platform drying

explanation: Mechanical press or chemical extraction. This is where the chemical half of the phrase mechanical and chemical operations comes from.

why.a: Correct. Palm kernel oil is obtained by mechanical pressing and chemical extraction.
why.b: Wrong. Boiling and skimming is clarification of crude palm oil.
why.c: Wrong. Those are stages in the fruit sequence.
why.d: Wrong. Those are drying methods for the nuts.

prompt: Palm kernel oil is obtained by mechanical pressing and by {{1}} extraction methods.
explanation: Chemical. It is the reason the unit introduction describes processing as mechanical and chemical operations.

prompt: How are palm kernel nuts and the extracted oil stored?

options.text: The nuts in big jute bags, and the oil in oil tanks
The nuts in oil tanks, and the oil in jute bags
Both in polythene bags
Both in cold rooms with backup generators

explanation: Jute bags for the nuts, tanks for the oil. Option B reverses them, which is the only trap available on a fact this simple.

why.a: Correct. Nuts in big jute bags, oil in oil tanks.
why.b: Wrong. This reverses the two.
why.c: Wrong. Polythene bags hold nursery seedlings.
why.d: Wrong. Cold rooms belong to the fish marketing unit.

prompt: Palm kernel nuts are usually stored in big {{1}} bags.
explanation: Jute. The glossary defines jute bags as sacks made of coarse fibre used for storing dried palm kernels.

prompt: Which four factors affect crude palm oil quality?

options.text: Harvesting time or fruit ripeness, sterilisation time and temperature, pressing conditions, and storage and handling
Soil pH, rainfall, temperature, and spacing
Variety, fruit type, pigment, and shell thickness
Market demand, cost of inputs, profit margin, and scalability

explanation: Ripeness, sterilisation, pressing, storage. Notice that three of the four are processing decisions and only the first is made in the field.

why.a: Correct. These four are the factors affecting oil quality.
why.b: Wrong. Those are the environmental requirements for cultivation.
why.c: Wrong. Those are classification features, not quality factors.
why.d: Wrong. Those are agribusiness evaluation criteria from Module Four.

prompt: The text names {{1}} factors that influence the quality of crude palm oil.
explanation: Four. Module Three counts to remember: 5 cultivation stages, 5 fruit processing stages, 5 kernel stages, 4 quality factors, 3 by-products.

prompt: What effect do overripe or under-ripe fruits have on oil quality?

options.text: They lead to poor oil quality with high free fatty acid levels
They raise the oil yield but darken the colour
They have no effect if sterilisation is done properly
They increase the smoke point of the oil

explanation: High free fatty acids, the standard marker of degraded oil. It is why the three ripeness signs in Unit 1 matter commercially and not just agronomically.

why.a: Correct. Overripe or under-ripe fruit gives poor oil quality with high FFA.
why.b: Wrong. Quality falls; no yield gain is claimed.
why.c: Wrong. Harvesting time is listed as a factor in its own right.
why.d: Wrong. Smoke point distinguishes palm kernel oil from palm oil.

prompt: Overripe or under-ripe fruits lead to poor oil quality with high {{1}} levels.
explanation: Free fatty acid, FFA. It is the one quality index used throughout Module Three.

prompt: What does the text say about over-steaming or under-steaming, and about pressing?

options.text: Over or under-steaming can affect oil yield and quality, and high-pressure pressing is key to extracting maximum oil without damaging quality
Steaming time has no effect once the correct temperature is reached
Low-pressure pressing gives the best quality oil
Pressing should be avoided in favour of chemical extraction

explanation: Both directions matter for steaming, and pressing wants high pressure without damaging the oil. Both are balancing acts rather than one-way rules.

why.a: Correct. Both halves come straight from the factors affecting oil quality.
why.b: Wrong. Sterilisation time is named alongside temperature.
why.c: Wrong. High-pressure pressing is what the text recommends.
why.d: Wrong. Chemical extraction is for kernel oil, not for the mesocarp.

prompt: Proper storage of the oil after extraction prevents {{1}} and spoilage.
explanation: Oxidation. The self-assessment answer expands it: exposure to air, heat and light causes oxidation and rancidity, giving off-flavours and reduced shelf life.

prompt: What are the three by-products of oil palm processing?

options.text: Empty fruit bunches, palm kernel cake, and palm oil mill effluent
Palm oil, palm kernel oil, and palm kernel meal
Fibre, shell, and stalk
Biogas, compost, and biodiesel

explanation: EFB, PKC, POME. Option B is the products rather than the by-products, and option D is what two of the by-products become.

why.a: Correct. These three are the by-products of processing.
why.b: Wrong. Those are the primary products of the crop.
why.c: Wrong. Fibre is a by-product, but this set is not the one the text names.
why.d: Wrong. Biogas and compost are what POME and EFB become, not the by-products themselves.

prompt: Oil palm processing generates {{1}} named by-products: EFB, PKC and POME.
explanation: Three. The cultivation unit lists five products and by-products together; the processing unit narrows to these three.

prompt: What are empty fruit bunches, and what two uses does the processing unit give them?

options.text: The bunches remaining after the fruit is stripped, used as fertiliser or in the production of bioenergy
The solid residue from the kernel, used as animal feed
The wastewater from extraction, requiring treatment
The fibrous residue after pressing, used as animal bedding

explanation: Fertiliser and bioenergy. The cultivation unit adds a third use, biodegradable building materials.

why.a: Correct. EFB are the stripped bunches, used as fertiliser or for bioenergy.
why.b: Wrong. That is palm kernel cake.
why.c: Wrong. That is POME.
why.d: Wrong. That is palm pressed fibre.

prompt: Empty fruit bunches are used as fertiliser and for {{1}}.
explanation: Bioenergy. Bedding belongs to palm pressed fibre and biodiesel to palm oil, so the three are easy to swap.

prompt: What is palm kernel cake in the processing unit, and what is it used for?

options.text: The solid residue from the kernel after oil extraction, used as animal feed
The stripped bunches, used as compost
The fibre from the mesocarp, used as fuel
The wastewater, used for irrigation without treatment

explanation: Solid residue from the kernel, animal feed. The in-text answer adds why: its nutritional content makes it valuable.

why.a: Correct. PKC is the solid residue from the kernel after oil extraction, used as animal feed.
why.b: Wrong. Those are empty fruit bunches.
why.c: Wrong. That is palm pressed fibre.
why.d: Wrong. POME requires treatment before discharge, so it cannot be used untreated.

prompt: Palm kernel cake is the solid {{1}} from the kernel after oil extraction.
explanation: Residue. Palm pressed fibre is also a residue, but the fibrous one from the mesocarp rather than the solid one from the kernel.

prompt: What is POME?

options.text: Palm oil mill effluent, the wastewater generated during oil extraction, which contains high levels of organic matter and requires treatment before discharge
Palm oil mill equipment, the machinery used in a mill
Processed oil for market export, the finished product
Palm oil mesocarp extract, a food additive

explanation: Palm Oil Mill Effluent. The word effluent is the giveaway: it is waste water, not a product.

why.a: Correct. POME is the wastewater from oil extraction, high in organic matter, requiring treatment.
why.b: Wrong. The abbreviation does not stand for equipment.
why.c: Wrong. POME is a waste stream, not a product.
why.d: Wrong. No such additive appears in the course.

prompt: POME stands for palm oil mill {{1}}.
explanation: Effluent. The deck's summary of it is short and quotable: requires treatment before disposal.

prompt: Why can untreated POME deplete oxygen in water bodies?

options.text: Because it has high biochemical oxygen demand and chemical oxygen demand
Because it raises the water temperature above 34 degrees Celsius
Because it contains iron bacteria that clog fish gills
Because it is acidic enough to kill all aquatic plants

explanation: High BOD and COD. Both are measures of how much oxygen the water will lose breaking down what has been discharged into it.

why.a: Correct. High biochemical and chemical oxygen demand deplete the oxygen in receiving waters.
why.b: Wrong. Temperature is not the mechanism given.
why.c: Wrong. Gallionella and Leptothrix are iron bacteria from the fish farming unit.
why.d: Wrong. Acidity is not the stated mechanism.

prompt: POME has high biochemical oxygen demand and {{1}} oxygen demand.
explanation: Chemical oxygen demand, COD. The pair BOD and COD is the technical core of the POME answer.

prompt: Besides oxygen depletion, which environmental concerns does POME raise?

options.text: Water pollution harming aquatic life, unpleasant odours, and greenhouse gas emissions of methane during decomposition
Soil compaction and dust generation
Noise pollution and light pollution
Ozone depletion and acid rain

explanation: Aquatic harm, odour, methane. The methane point is why anaerobic digestion into biogas is offered as the sustainable answer: it captures the gas instead of releasing it.

why.a: Correct. These three are named in the self-assessment answer.
why.b: Wrong. Neither appears in connection with POME.
why.c: Wrong. Neither appears in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Neither appears in the course.

prompt: Which two sustainable practices does the text give for managing palm oil by-products?

options.text: Biogas production using anaerobic digesters on POME, and composting empty fruit bunches and other solid residues
Landfilling POME and burning empty fruit bunches
Discharging POME into rivers after settling, and selling EFB as fuel
Drying POME into powder and pressing EFB into board

explanation: Biogas and compost. Both turn a disposal problem into a product, which is agricultural waste management from Module One applied to palm.

why.a: Correct. Anaerobic digestion of POME into biogas, and composting of EFB and solid residues.
why.b: Wrong. Neither is offered, and burning wastes the material.
why.c: Wrong. POME requires treatment before discharge, not settling and release.
why.d: Wrong. Biodegradable building materials are a cultivation-unit use of EFB, but this pair is not the sustainable practice named.

prompt: POME can be converted into biogas using {{1}} digesters.
explanation: Anaerobic, meaning without oxygen. That is the condition under which methane forms, which is why capturing it is both an environmental and an energy gain.

prompt: Effective management and recycling of processing by-products is essential for reducing the environmental impact of palm oil processing.
explanation: The closing sentence of the by-products section, and the reason biogas and composting appear in the self-assessment answers.

why.true: Correct. The text says effective management and recycling of by-products is essential.
why.false: Wrong. This contradicts the section's own conclusion.

prompt: Why is threshing an important step in palm oil processing?

options.text: It separates fruit from the bunch stalks, ensures maximum recovery of the oil-rich mesocarp, and keeps stalks and debris out of the extraction phase
It kills the pathogens on the fruit surface
It reduces the moisture content of the nuts
It removes water and sludge from the crude oil

explanation: Three reasons: separation, recovery, and purity of what enters extraction. It is the self-assessment answer in full.

why.a: Correct. These three reasons are given in the self-assessment answer.
why.b: Wrong. Killing pathogens is sterilisation.
why.c: Wrong. Reducing moisture is nut drying.
why.d: Wrong. Removing water and sludge is clarification.

prompt: What are the consequences of improper storage and handling of crude palm oil?

options.text: Oxidation and rancidity, contamination by dirt, water or microorganisms, and loss of quality from temperature fluctuations and moisture
A rise in the free fatty acid level only, with no other effect
An increase in the oil's smoke point
Improved shelf life through natural fermentation

explanation: Three consequences: oxidation and rancidity, contamination, and quality loss. Off-flavours and reduced shelf life follow from the first.

why.a: Correct. These three are named in the self-assessment answer.
why.b: Wrong, and the word only cuts out two of the three consequences.
why.c: Wrong. Degradation does not raise the smoke point.
why.d: Wrong. Rancidity shortens shelf life rather than extending it.

prompt: How does the glossary define free fatty acids?

options.text: Substances that form when oil degrades, indicating poor quality if levels are high
The healthy unsaturated fats found in fish
The pigments that give palm oil its colour
The residues left in the press after extraction

explanation: A degradation product, and a quality indicator. High FFA means the oil has been mishandled somewhere between the field and the tank.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry.
why.b: Wrong. Those are omega-3 fatty acids, from the fish farming unit.
why.c: Wrong. Pigments are carotenoid and anthocyanin.
why.d: Wrong. Press residues are palm pressed fibre.

prompt: Free fatty acids form when oil {{1}}, and high levels indicate poor quality.
explanation: Degrades. Sterilisation exists partly to stop this by inactivating the enzymes responsible.

prompt: What is biogas, according to the glossary?

options.text: A renewable energy source produced from the decomposition of organic waste like palm oil mill effluent
A fuel refined from crude palm oil
The gas released when jute bags decompose
A fertiliser made from empty fruit bunches

explanation: Renewable energy from decomposing organic waste, with POME named as the example. Biodiesel, by contrast, is made from palm oil itself.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry for biogas.
why.b: Wrong. That describes biodiesel.
why.c: Wrong. Jute bags are storage sacks.
why.d: Wrong. Composted EFB is a fertiliser, but that is compost rather than biogas.

prompt: What does the deck give as the conclusion of oil palm processing?

options.text: It ensures the production of edible oil, industrial raw materials, and valuable by-products
It produces edible oil and nothing else of value
It is only worthwhile at industrial scale
It has been replaced by chemical synthesis

explanation: Three outputs: edible oil, industrial raw materials, and valuable by-products. The by-products are what make the process sustainable rather than wasteful.

why.a: Correct. This is the deck's closing statement.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. By-products are a whole section of the unit.
why.c: Wrong. Sterilisation in pots and drums shows the smallholder route.
why.d: Wrong. No such claim appears anywhere.

prompt: Oil palm processing is a critical component of the global {{1}} oil market.
explanation: Vegetable oil market. Palm oil is described in Unit 1 as one of the most widely used vegetable oils in the world.

prompt: Match each operation to the sequence it belongs to.
explanation: Two sequences of five, easily blurred. Anything to do with the nut, its fibre, its drying or its cracking belongs to the kernel line.
